chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated to us, he said: Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad narrated to us from Ali, from Abu Basir, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say:

A servant will be brought on the Day of Judgment having offered prayer, so he will say: 'O Lord, I prayed seeking Your pleasure.' He will be told: 'Rather, you prayed so that it would be said: How good is the prayer of so-and-so!' 'Take him to the Fire!' And a servant who fought will be brought, and he will say: 'O Lord, I fought seeking Your pleasure.' He will be told: 'Rather, you fought so that it would be said: How brave is so-and!' 'Take him to the Fire!' And a servant who learned the Quran will be brought, and he will say: 'O Lord, I learned the Quran seeking Your pleasure.' He will be told: 'Rather, you learned it so that it would be said: How good is the voice of so-and-so!' 'Take him to the Fire!' And a servant who spent his wealth will be brought, and he will say: 'O Lord, I spent my wealth seeking Your pleasure.' He will be told: 'Rather, you spent it so that it would be said: How generous is so-and-so!' 'Take him to the Fire!'
ai.seo_question: What happens to acts of worship if done for show rather than sincerity?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kitab al-Zuhd* highlights the Shia emphasis on *ikhlas* (sincerity) by demonstrating that even valid acts like prayer, jihad, Quran recitation, and charity can be nullified if motivated by a desire for human acclaim (*al-hamd*) rather than pure devotion to God. It underscores the subtle danger of self-admiration, where the worshipper becomes the audience for their own piety, leading to spiritual ruin despite outward correctness.
